sections.html:
Selling to a buyer who takes the house as it stands is the fastest option in Manitowoc, since repairs and showings are what drag out a typical listing. An agent listing and a private sale are the other choices. All three finish with a condition report from you, a state transfer return and a recorded deed.

Prices in Manitowoc are low. A typical owner-occupied home is worth $160,700, and owners live in 67.6% of homes. With values like that, a few thousand dollars of postponed repair can be a big share of the price, so many sellers compare an as-is sale with fixing the house first.

Manitowoc is the county seat, on Lake Michigan where the Manitowoc River meets it. Use these citywide numbers as a quick read on local housing.

sections.h2: Do Manitowoc landlords have to register a rental before selling?
sections.html:
If the house has been a rental, you must be on file with the city. Ordinance 16.140 makes owners of residential rental units give their contact details to Building Inspection, at no charge. The registration stays with the current owner, so the buyer registers again after a change of ownership.

  • Register a new rental unit within 30 days of occupancy.
  • Report contact changes within 30 days.
  • A missed deadline can mean a forfeiture of up to $100 per rental unit, with each week of noncompliance a separate offense.
  • Buildings with three or more units still get an annual common-area inspection from the Fire Department.

Send forms to Building Inspection, 900 Quay Street, or call (920) 686-6940 with questions. A vacant duplex still counts, so bring the paperwork up to date before a buyer asks.

Short-term rentals follow different rules than standard rentals. A tourist rooming house skips the city's rental registration and instead gets its license from the Manitowoc County Health Department, (920) 683-4155. Zoning allows short-term rentals in districts R-1 through R-7 and B-1, and the city Finance Department handles room tax questions at (920) 686-6960.

An open permit can cause trouble at closing. Inspections need 24 hours' notice on business days, and a permit that expires without a final inspection gets archived as incomplete, leaving the work unapproved. If a deck, furnace or bathroom project never received its final, call Building Inspection before you list so the buyer does not find the gap first.

Each permit lists the inspections it needs. For building work the city uses these types:

  • Footing, ahead of the concrete pour.
  • Foundation, ahead of backfilling.
  • Rough in, ahead of insulation or drywall covering the framing.
  • Insulation, covering installed insulation and vapor retarders.
  • Final and final occupancy, which confirm code compliance before the space is used.

sections.h2: Assessments and the Board of Review
sections.html:
Value is set by the City Assessor as of January 1, following Chapter 70 of the state statutes, with Associated Appraisal Consultants doing the city's work. Late spring brings Open Book sessions, and the Board of Review sits at City Hall in early summer. Exact dates change yearly, so phone the Assessor's office.

The Assessor neither sets tax rates nor collects tax, and values are adjusted to market using open sales every other year. If a letter arrives asking you to verify property details, answer it, since that data feeds your valuation when you sell.

Condition and timing point the way. A tidy house and a flexible schedule favor a listing and the wider buyer pool it brings. A house that needs work, a tenant, an estate, or a firm move date favors a cash buyer, who will usually trade some price for speed.

When you compare offers, ask each buyer to put in writing the price, who pays closing costs, and the closing date they can meet. Placed side by side, those three items show which offer actually leaves you better off.

Start with the documents a buyer will ask for first. Your latest tax bill carries the parcel number the deed needs. Permit records and receipts show that decks, furnaces and bathrooms were done properly. If the house has been a rental, have your registration details ready, and for a short-term rental, your health department license and room tax records.

Then tour the house with the condition report beside you. Record what you know about the roof, basement, plumbing and wiring, and about wells, septic systems and storage tanks if your lot is outside city services. A clear list lets a cash buyer name a price without delay.

sections.h2: From signed contract to closing day
sections.html:
The contract date starts the 10-day clock for the report, so write it down. After that the tasks run side by side: the title company runs a records search, your lender is asked for a payoff figure, and both parties complete the electronic transfer return.

At closing the signed deed travels to the Register of Deeds with the return receipt, and your mortgage payoff and tax share are taken from the proceeds. Because a cash buyer needs no lender, the date can often follow your move. Borrowers add an appraisal and loan approval, which stretches the timeline. If a date slips, tell the title company at once so that deadlines tied to the contract are not missed.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or inherited house
sections.html:
Tenants generally remain until the lease runs out. Look up the end date and notice terms before promising a closing day, and if the buyer wants an empty house, agree the move-out with the tenant.

With an inherited house, begin by confirming who may sign for the estate. Then ask Building Inspection what remains open, because the city treats an expired permit as incomplete work. Clearing those items early gives a buyer fewer reasons to hesitate, and it keeps a family sale from stalling over a technicality.

Two state statutes shape your sale. Wis. Stat. 77.22 charges the seller 30 cents per $100 of value as a transfer fee, and Wis. Stat. 709.02 requires a condition report for one-to-four unit property within 10 days of contract acceptance, failing which the buyer may rescind. The form covers wells, septic systems and storage tanks, so collect that information early if your lot lies outside city services.

Deeds go to the Manitowoc County Register of Deeds in the Courthouse, 1010 S 8th Street, Room 107. Hours are Monday 8:30 to 5:00 and Tuesday through Friday 8:30 to 4:30. File the transfer return electronically with the Department of Revenue and bring the printed receipt along with the signed deed.

faqs.q: Is there a fee to register a rental in Manitowoc?
faqs.a: It costs nothing. The Residential Rental Contact Registration is a one-time filing, contact changes are reported within 30 days, and a buyer files a new registration after the sale.

faqs.q: Who issues a short-term rental license in Manitowoc?
faqs.a: The Manitowoc County Health Department, at (920) 683-4155, does the pre-licensing inspection and issues the tourist rooming house license. The city's Building Inspection office, at (920) 686-6940, confirms zoning.

faqs.q: What if a Manitowoc permit never got a final inspection?
faqs.a: When a permit expires without a final, the city archives the project as incomplete and treats the work as unapproved. Ask Building Inspection what is open before selling and close it out first.

faqs.q: What is the Wisconsin transfer fee on a Manitowoc sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays 30 cents on each $100 of value when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Manitowoc?
faqs.a: Manitowoc County Courthouse, 1010 S 8th Street, 1st Floor, Room 107. It is open Monday from 8:30 to 5:00 and the rest of the week from 8:30 to 4:30.
